about: A story as a small graph: claims, each with its label, who said it, when, and the rows and data fields that support it. The page is generated from this file by tools/stories-build.mjs; nothing here is new reporting. See stories/grammar.md.
title: Who warned first, and how long before
standfirst: For Lisbon's worst hours on Wednesday, who said what, in what order, and how many hours ahead: IPMA, civil protection, the government, Web Summit. Every time is the issuer's own where the data room has it.

warnings_in_force.about: The official warnings a story about the storm states first, drawn as the front page draws them: for each kind of weather IPMA's newest message by the time it was sent (cap.json beside this file), saying what IPMA's open-data feed (this file) lists where the two differ; resolved when the page is built and read again in the reader's browser. Never a level of our own.

sections.title: The weather service and civil protection
The wind warning, which was lowered

claims.text: The first signal for the mainland was IPMA's: communiqué no. 1 named the storm on Monday 9 November at 13:17, said orange warnings would follow and did not rule out an upgrade. That is 46.7 hours before Lisbon's red wind warning begins, at 12:00 on Wednesday.
claims.label: fact

supports.field: lead_times[warning=storm named, orange expected, upgrade possible].lead_hours

claims.text: Ten minutes later, at 13:27, IPMA sent a wind warning message for the Lisbon district. Its level is no longer in the feed: it is the message the red warning later replaced.
claims.label: fact

contains: its level is not in the feed any more

claims.text: Civil protection came next: ANEPC's public warning, Aviso 21, on Monday at 20:30, 39.5 hours ahead, before any red warning existed.
claims.label: fact

claims.text: IPMA sent the red wind warning for Lisbon on Tuesday at 07:18:40, for Wednesday 12:00 to 21:00: 28.7 hours ahead. It stood just under 24 hours: at 07:16:30 on Wednesday IPMA replaced it with an orange wind warning from 09:00 to 21:00, sent 1 hour 44 minutes before that begins.
claims.label: fact

contains: sent 1 h 44 min before the new orange begins

claims.text: The press we could read had it 47 minutes later (Diário de Notícias' live blog, 08:05), and Lusa's piece gave the warning's time as 08:31: about an hour and a quarter after IPMA sent it.
claims.label: evidence
claims.said_by: Diário de Notícias (live blog); Lusa, as published by AWAY

claims.text: The government followed IPMA by about two hours: the Interior Minister announced the alert situation at ANEPC's press conference, reported from 09:14 to 09:17 on Tuesday; the minute he spoke is not established.
claims.label: evidence
claims.said_by: the Interior Minister, as reported by Observador's and Diário de Notícias' live blogs

claims.text: The government's own page with the measures is timed 12:10. The alert situation covers Wednesday from 00:00 to 23:59.
claims.label: fact

claims.text: The rain warning came later and then moved. IPMA first made Lisbon's rain red at 16:30 on Tuesday, for 12:00 on Wednesday: 19.5 hours ahead. At 21:23 it moved the start to 09:00, which left 11.6 hours; the orange rain before it was moved to 00:00, 2.6 hours ahead.
claims.label: fact

claims.text: IPMA's own open-data feed ran behind its warnings: the 21:23 change appeared there only between 23:22 and 23:51, at least two hours later.
claims.label: fact

contains: lagged the CAP messages by at least 2 h

claims.text: That move to 09:00 had not been reported in any article title or live-blog entry the media watch could read by 00:15 on Wednesday. The first press text it has since read that gives Lisbon's red rain from 09:00 is an entry in Observador's live blog at 08:46:16 on Wednesday: 11 hours 23 minutes after IPMA sent the change, and 14 minutes before the warning began. The entry presents the red rain as newly issued, not as moved.
claims.label: hypothesis
claims.confidence: limited by method: the first text the media desk read, found by hand at 09:38; an earlier one it could not read may exist (some outlets refuse automated reads)

claims.text: Web Summit's decision came last. First the government's recommendation to suspend Wednesday, reported at 17:53 on Tuesday, with the decision left to the organisers.
claims.label: evidence
claims.said_by: the Government, as reported by Jornal de Negócios' live blog (no government page was found)

claims.text: Then the organisers' own page, published at 19:09: "Day 2 (Wednesday, November 11th) will not take place".
claims.label: fact

claims.text: Set in order, with the hours between: IPMA's red wind warning (07:18), the government's alert about two hours after it, the government's recommendation to Web Summit ten and a half hours after it (17:53), the organisers' decision 11 hours 50 minutes after it (19:09).
claims.label: evidence
claims.said_by: this desk, subtracting the times in the sentences it names

claims.text: The press had the organisers' decision 32 minutes after the page went up: ECO at 19:41.
claims.label: evidence

claims.text: Was there an earlier sign? Our meteorologist's hypothesis: the low the US National Hurricane Center followed from 2 November, labelled AL94 on 6 November and dropped on 8 November, was absorbed by the low that became CHARLES. If so, a precursor about nine days ahead: in the analysis's words, "weak signals, not warnings". Its status there: "not established".
claims.label: hypothesis
claims.said_by: incident.meteorologist@web-summit.dinis (analysis; not IPMA's or NHC's words)

supports.expect: the new non-tropical low that absorbed AL94 is, or became part of, CHARLES

claims.text: The wind warning that came first was later lowered. On Wednesday at 07:16:30 IPMA sent eleven messages for the mainland: red to orange, 09:00 to 21:00, for Lisboa, Setúbal and Beja; red to yellow, 12:00 to 21:00, for Leiria, Santarém, Portalegre and Évora; orange to yellow for Guarda, Castelo Branco and Coimbra; and a new yellow thunderstorm warning for Faro. For Lisbon that was 1 hour 44 minutes before the new window opened, and it opened three hours earlier than the red one would have.
claims.label: fact
claims.said_by: IPMA, CAP messages read through MeteoAlarm

claims.text: What stayed red after that change: on the mainland a red wind warning only for Faro (09:00 to 21:00), and red rain warnings in eight districts: Lisboa, Setúbal, Beja and Faro (09:00 to 18:00), Santarém, Leiria, Castelo Branco and Portalegre (12:00 to 18:00), as IPMA's open data had it when read at 08:47. Lisbon's red rain warning, sent on Tuesday at 21:23, was not touched.
claims.label: fact
claims.said_by: IPMA, open data and CAP messages

not_known.text: The minute the Interior Minister announced the alert situation: 09:14 is the earliest report; the government's page is timed 12:10.
The level of IPMA's first wind message for Lisbon (9 November, 13:27): it left the feed when the red warning replaced it.
The exact minutes between Web Summit's page (19:09:00) and ECO (19:41:31): the timeline says 32 minutes, the media watch's table 33. This story says about half an hour.
When the government told Web Summit: its recommendation is known only from the press (first report 17:53); no government page was found.
Whether these lead times were enough. That is a judgement, not in the data room, and not made here.
Madeira's warnings and what was measured there: a story of its own, to come.

record.what: First telling, on the data read at 02:22:46 UTC: 15 sentences.

One sentence made exact. Before: the press had the decision "about half an hour" after the page, while the timeline (32 minutes) and the media desk's table (33) disagreed. Now: 32 minutes; the media desk's table states its rule (whole minutes elapsed) and gives 32.

One sentence retold after IPMA lowered Lisbon's wind warning. Before: the red wind warning, sent Tuesday 07:18:40, 28.7 hours ahead. Now also: replaced at 07:16:30 on Wednesday by an orange warning from 09:00 (row s-1111T0738). The lead times counted to 12:00 elsewhere in this story are to the start the red warning had.

The box at the top is now drawn from both of IPMA's channels, as the front page draws it: the newest message for each kind of weather, and what the open-data feed still lists where the two differ (before, it was drawn from the open data alone and showed red wind after IPMA's 07:16 message had lowered it to orange).
Added from row s-1111T0824: the whole of IPMA's 07:16:30 change across the mainland (w15) and what stayed red after it (w16). Nothing said before was changed.

Retold on the media desk's table of 09:39:39 UTC. Before, w10 said: "That move to 09:00 had not been reported in any article title or live-blog entry the media watch could read by 00:15 on Wednesday." Now: the table counts one press text, Observador's live entry of 08:46:16 on Wednesday, 683 minutes after IPMA's message.
